reference.note: Generated by contracts/suede-vocal.ts. Do not hand-edit; run the regenerate command in contracts/README.md.

Countertenor.caveat: A countertenor's working transition is the crossing out of full voice into the falsetto-family register the voice then sings above — a different event from the shifts listed for the other categories, and the one figure here that varies most from singer to singer.

pitchHz.note: NSDF (McLeod-Wyvill) with parabolic interpolation, monophonic, one f0 per frame.

centsFromTarget.note: Signed deviation from a named target pitch. The strongest measurement the app has.

inTuneHoldTime.note: Time held inside the tolerance window, latency-corrected before it is credited.

scorePercent.note: In-tolerance hold time over possible hold time.

sustainSeconds.note: Longest continuous above-threshold tone. RMS-gated, so it counts an unvoiced hiss too.

loudnessSteadiness.note: 1 minus the coefficient of variation of RMS. This is a LOUDNESS measure. It is not airflow and it is not pitch.

phonationSeconds.note: Confidently voiced time. Counts singing rather than time with the page open. An unvoiced hiss reads as zero here.

cycleDose.note: f0 integrated over phonation time. Load evidence, with no published safe ceiling.

rangeExtremes.note: Lowest and highest comfortable note by cumulative dwell. Falsetto and head voice count toward the high note.

ringRatio.note: Share of energy in a fixed 2800-3200 Hz band. Self-relative only: compare a singer against their own takes, never against a target or another singer. NOT a strain measure.

unbrokenPhraseLength.note: The voiced/unvoiced trace already carries this; no function reduces it to a longest-run number.

onsetTimingError.note: The latency model needed to do this honestly exists, but there is no onset detector and no timing-error number.

vibratoRateHz.note: No analysis of the f0 contour's periodicity. The data to build it is captured; zero code exists.

strainOrPressedPhonation.note: No jitter, shimmer, HNR or CPP anywhere in any Suede surface. Not cheaply buildable. Do not substitute ringRatio for it.

registerMechanism.note: No chest/head/falsetto classification on any Suede surface. This row used to say the iOS app reports a single H1-H2 derived boundary; that was false and is corrected here — the iOS app has no spectral analysis at all, its pitch estimator is time-domain YIN, and its only vocal surface plots f0 and latches range extremes. `lib/audio/register-mechanism.ts` now computes H1-H2 as a pure function against one boundary that is chosen rather than validated, and nothing calls it from a live take. Even once something does, the boundary it settles is the heavier laryngeal mechanism against the lighter; the pedagogical chest and head both sit inside the heavier one, so it will not answer a chest-versus-head question.

vowelOrFormant.note: One fixed band ratio is the whole of the spectral analysis. No formant tracking, so vowel consistency cannot be scored.

absoluteLoudness.note: Input RMS is uncalibrated. Disabling AGC makes it stable, not absolute, so discrete dynamic levels are not measurable.

simultaneousVoices.note: The detector returns one f0 per frame. A harmony sung against a lead is not two measurable parts.

passaggioPitches.note: See taxonomy.passaggio.derivableFromRangeScan. The published zones are per-category, not personal, and a range scan does not imply them.

flow-consistency.claimedAs: airflow or flow steadiness during a sustain
flow-consistency.reality: loudnessSteadiness is a coefficient of variation of LOUDNESS, not of airflow.

pitch-steadiness-in-breath-room.claimedAs: the breath room watching how steady the pitch stays
pitch-steadiness-in-breath-room.reality: The sustain test reads frame volume only and never reads f0. No cents drift is measured in the breath room at all.

personal-passaggio-from-range-scan.claimedAs: both passaggio pitches computed from a range scan
personal-passaggio-from-range-scan.reality: A range scan returns a low note, a high note and an estimated category label. Passaggio zones are published per category.

strain-free-verdict.claimedAs: a pass/fail that the singer was not straining
strain-free-verdict.reality: No strain detector exists. A strain claim cannot be scored, only self-reported.

held-harmony-against-a-lead.claimedAs: a harmony line measured against a simultaneous lead

book.title: The Measured Voice
book.subtitle: A practical guide to building a voice you can measure — included with Suede Sing Pro.

chapters.title: What your voice actually is
chapters.summary: Breath as the power, the folds as the vibrator, the throat and mouth as the filter — the three-part model the rest of this book runs on.

chapters.title: Registers, and why they exist
chapters.summary: What physically changes between chest, head, mix, falsetto and whistle — and why teachers give the same sounds different names.

chapters.title: The passaggio: where it breaks and why
chapters.summary: Why your voice has a transition zone, roughly where it sits for your voice type, and why vowel and weight get you through it when force never will.

chapters.title: Breath: support versus pressure
chapters.summary: What support actually means physically, why pushing more air makes tone worse, and how to feel the difference.

chapters.title: Resonance, placement and the vowel
chapters.summary: How the throat and mouth shape one buzzy fold vibration into vowels, brightness and carrying power — and how to change tone without changing effort.

chapters.title: Stamina, warming up, and not hurting yourself
chapters.summary: What warming up and cooling down actually do, how water and sleep really reach your voice, and where normal tiredness ends and a doctor begins.

chapters.title: Your range is not one number
chapters.summary: Your voice has three ranges — absolute, comfortable, and performable — and the one people quote is the least useful of the three.

chapters.title: Reading your range test
chapters.summary: How to take the range test honestly, what a disappointing result usually means, and how much the voice-type label is worth.

chapters.title: What pitch accuracy actually measures
chapters.summary: How to read an accuracy score honestly: what a cent is, why dead centre isn't the goal, and how drift, scoops and vibrato differ.

chapters.title: Finding your own break on the chart
chapters.summary: How to locate your own transition with the pitch studio and range test, read a belt ceiling honestly, and tell head voice from falsetto.

chapters.title: Tracking change over months, not days
chapters.summary: How to tell real vocal change from ordinary day-to-day noise, and how long to wait before your progress charts mean anything.

chapters.title: When the numbers lie to you
chapters.summary: How room noise, mic placement, headphone bleed and a rough day distort your readings — and how to catch a bad session before you act on it.

chapters.title: How the twelve weeks work
chapters.summary: The shape of the twelve weeks — four blocks, short sessions, and the rules for skipping, repeating, and going back.

chapters.title: Weeks 1 and 2: baseline and breath
chapters.summary: How to spend the first two weeks collecting honest data and building a breath habit, without trying to sing better yet.

chapters.title: Weeks 3 and 4: the middle voice
chapters.summary: Two weeks in the part of your range that already works: steady tone, clean onsets, honest sustain, and the ear work that holds them together.

chapters.title: Weeks 5 and 6: through the break
chapters.summary: Two weeks of quiet sirens, slides and vowel work across your transition — how to run the sessions, and what to do when they go badly.

chapters.title: Weeks 7 and 8: extending the top
chapters.summary: How to work above your transition for two weeks: height without weight, head voice before belt, and hard limits on volume and repetition.

chapters.title: Weeks 9 and 10: the bottom and the long phrase
chapters.summary: Two weeks on the low register, which rewards release rather than effort, and on carrying a long phrase without running the tank dry.

chapters.title: Weeks 11 and 12: putting it in a song
chapters.summary: Move the last two weeks onto real repertoire, retest, and compare against your week-one recording without fooling yourself.

chapters.title: Choosing songs that actually fit
chapters.summary: How to audit a song before you learn it: where its melody lives, why the chorus decides, and what the highest note is really telling you.

chapters.title: Transposition without shame
chapters.summary: Why changing a song's key is ordinary professional practice, how to find the key that fits you, and where transposition stops helping.

chapters.title: Learning from other singers' ranges
chapters.summary: How to read the singer library for tessitura and craft instead of ceilings, and what those cited figures can and cannot tell you.

chapters.title: Building a set you can survive
chapters.summary: How to order songs, keys and rest across a whole set so your voice is still working on the last song.

atlas.title: The Voice Atlas
atlas.subtitle: Who sings what, how it sounds, and how to borrow it — the range, tone and technique of every voice in the library.

chapters.title: How to read an entry
chapters.summary: The anatomy of an atlas entry — what the cited range, the full-voice ceiling, the whistle flag and the sourced extremes actually claim, and how conservative those claims are.

chapters.title: Notes, octaves and the keyboard
chapters.summary: Scientific pitch notation in five minutes — what C4 means, why F#5 and Gb5 are the same note, how octave spans are counted, and why identical voices get different figures.

chapters.title: Voice types in the wild
chapters.summary: What the eight classification labels mean, why a pop mezzo and an opera mezzo are different claims, tessitura versus range, and how to guess your own type without a teacher.

chapters.title: A vocabulary for tone
chapters.summary: The working lexicon behind every entry — weight, placement, vibrato, onset, grit, breathiness, twang, cry and their friends, each defined by ear with exemplars from the atlas.

chapters.title: How to borrow a voice
chapters.summary: The five-step method behind every technique paragraph in this book: pick a trait, match the habitat, change one dial at a time, close the loop with recordings, and time-box the costume.

chapters.title: The safety rail
chapters.summary: The four expensive things in this book — whistle notes, extreme lows, distortion and sustained belting — what makes each risky to chase, and the warning signs that mean stop.

chapters.title: Pop women: the founders
chapters.summary: The women who defined what a pop lead vocal is — from torch-song discipline through the belt arms race — and what their entries teach about power built to last.

chapters.title: Pop women: the moderns
chapters.summary: The current and recent generation of pop leads — whisper-pop, fry onsets, whistle flexes and conversational belts — and how the microphone rewrote what counts as power.

chapters.title: The pop men
chapters.summary: From crooners to falsetto-forward streaming stars — why the male pop lead keeps climbing, and what the tenor arms race costs the baritones who enter it.

chapters.title: The classic rock men
chapters.summary: The wailers, shouters and art-rock baritones of rock's imperial decades — where the famous highs really came from, and the era's quiet lesson about sustainable volume.

chapters.title: The women of rock
chapters.summary: Belters, banshees and deadpan cool — the women who fronted rock bands on their own terms, and why their entries are the atlas's best course in projection over a loud stage.

chapters.title: Alternative, punk and new wave
chapters.summary: From post-punk monotone to grunge catharsis — the chapter where refusing to sing beautifully became its own technique, and what that refusal actually requires.

chapters.title: Metal
chapters.summary: Air-raid tenors, operatic sopranos and controlled growls — the most technically demanding shouting on earth, and why metal singing is closer to opera than either camp admits.

chapters.title: The soul men
chapters.summary: Church-trained tenors, velvet baritones and the falsetto tradition — the men who made secular music testify, and the phrasing lessons every genre stole from them.

chapters.title: The soul and R&B women
chapters.summary: From torch and church to quiet storm — the women who set the bar for vocal authority, and why this chapter contains the atlas's densest concentration of complete techniques.

chapters.title: Modern R&B
chapters.summary: The streaming era's R&B — falsetto confessions, whisper-runs, baritone outliers and produced nonchalance — and how the genre traded the shout for the microphone's trust.

chapters.title: Gospel and a cappella
chapters.summary: The source tradition and the ensemble athletes — where the runs, the shout and the squall come from, plus the a cappella specialists who turned blend itself into virtuosity.

chapters.title: Country
chapters.summary: Twang as technology, the accent as instrument, and storytelling tessitura — country's vocal toolkit from honky-tonk cries to stadium baritones.

chapters.title: Folk and the songwriters
chapters.summary: The confiders — voices built to serve words, from coffeehouse sopranos to gravel philosophers — and why limited instruments produced unlimited careers here.

chapters.title: Jazz and the standards
chapters.summary: Horn-players with lyrics — time feel, delayed vibrato, harmonic ears and the microphone's first great singers, from the songbook era to the new jazz generation.

chapters.title: Opera and classical crossover
chapters.summary: The unamplified athletes — what filling a hall without a microphone actually requires, why opera ranges look modest, and what every amplified singer can steal from the fach system.

chapters.title: Musical theatre
chapters.summary: Eight shows a week — the belt as a certified skill, legit versus contemporary technique, and why theatre singers are the book's masters of sustainable intensity.

chapters.title: Latin voices
chapters.summary: From ranchera's long breath to reggaetón's rhythmic speech — a continent of vocal traditions, their signature techniques, and the bilingual generation remixing all of them.

chapters.title: K-pop, J-pop and global pop
chapters.summary: The idol-system technicians, Japan's genre-fluent stylists, playback legends and global outliers — precision singing at industrial standards.

chapters.title: Reggae, Afrobeats and African voices
chapters.summary: Groove-first singing — patois phrasing, Afrobeats' melodic economy, amapiano's smoothness and the continent's great griot and mbalax voices.

chapters.title: The records
chapters.summary: The atlas's extremes in one place — lowest floors, highest ceilings, widest spans and the whistle club, each with the recording where the note happened when one is famously known.

chapters.title: Every voice by type
chapters.summary: The whole library shelved by classification, basses to sopranos, with each voice's cited range — the shopping index for borrowing along your own shelf.

rules.voiceTypeIsEstimate: A range scan shows which conventional band overlaps a result. It cannot diagnose or permanently classify a voice, and no lesson may present the label as settled.
rules.passaggioIsPublishedNotMeasured: Passaggio zones are per-category published bands. Male rows are Miller's primo and secondo, exactly five semitones apart. Female rows are contemporary-commercial break figures, three to four semitones wide, and must not be relabelled as Miller's primo and secondo. Countertenor carries a required caveat instead of a confident number.
rules.rangeScanOutputs: A range scan yields lowMidi, highMidi and an estimated voice type label. It yields nothing else, and in particular no passaggio and no register boundary.
rules.workingRangeIsTrimmed: The scan records extremes reached by pushing. A usable working range trims the edges; the scan and the working range are different numbers and a curriculum must not call the scan 'the one you can use'.
rules.sustainIsLoudnessNotPitch: Sustain steadiness is the coefficient of variation of loudness. The breath room never reads f0.
rules.freeExerciseGate: A warmup is free if and only if it is in EXERCISES. Pro packs are gated by array membership, not by a flag, so a free surface must never deep-link a pack exercise.

classifiableVoiceTypes.reason: The classifier can return six categories; the editorial taxonomy publishes eight. Bass-baritone and countertenor have atlas pages and passaggio rows but are not reachable classifier outputs. Recorded so a consumer routing on a classified label knows two published categories can never arrive.

pitchToleranceCents.reason: Sung-note judgment is deliberately more forgiving than a fretted-instrument lesson check, and a tuner is stricter than both. Same key name, three different jobs; not a drift to collapse.

starScales.reason: Practice rooms grade on three stars at percentage floors; the songbook grades on five linear stars plus a letter. Two instruments, not one drifted number. A consumer asserting 'stars' must say which.
